THE PROBLEM WE ARE SOLVING

Space survival is a system of trade-offs.

Young learners often see space exploration as rockets and planets. A real mission also depends on difficult connected decisions: every astronaut needs oxygen, water, power, food, communication, safe shelter, and protection from radiation. Improving one system can consume resources from another.

Challenge statement in simple words

Build an interactive app that lets students operate a lunar or Martian outpost. They must experience how decisions about life support, radiation shielding, electricity, and food production decide whether a mission succeeds or fails.

❓

Problem

Space concepts can feel too complex, distant, or like memorisation.

→
🧠

Our solution

Students learn through explanations, guided choices, simulations, questions, and an AI assistant.

→
🧑‍🚀

Impact

Learners build systems thinking, science confidence, decision-making, and curiosity about exploration.

CORE ASTRONAUT KNOWLEDGE

Five systems every outpost needs.

A habitat is not one machine. It is a connected ecosystem. If power fails, water recycling and air systems can fail too.

⚡

Power

Electricity runs lights, computers, communication, heaters, water systems, oxygen systems, and greenhouses.

TECHNOLOGY ATLAS • REAL ENGINEERING, MADE UNDERSTANDABLE

The technologies that could make an outpost possible.

Explore the engineering behind a future Moon or Mars habitat. Each card explains the basic science, how the technology works, why it matters, and the challenge engineers still need to solve.

🧊
RESOURCE UTILISATION

ISRU: use local resources

How it works: In-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) means collecting and processing materials already at the destination, such as water ice or surface minerals.

Why it matters: Local resources could reduce the amount of water, oxygen, fuel, and construction material launched from Earth.

Engineering challenge: Finding, extracting, purifying, and processing useful material in harsh conditions is difficult. Many systems remain under development.

💧
WATER SYSTEMS

Water recovery & purification

How it works: Filters, separators, and treatment stages recover water from used water streams, then monitor its quality before reuse.

Why it matters: Water is heavy to launch. Recycling can reduce resupply needs and support drinking, hygiene, and plant growth.

Engineering challenge: Filters need maintenance, contaminants must be monitored, and backup supplies are still essential.

🫧
AIR & OXYGEN

Oxygen generation & electrolysis

How it works: Electrolysis uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Oxygen can support breathable-air systems after careful conditioning and monitoring.

Why it matters: It can help make oxygen from stored or recovered water instead of carrying every supply from Earth.

Engineering challenge: It needs reliable power, water purification, gas storage, leak detection, and redundant safety controls.

🔴
PLANETARY SCIENCE

MOXIE: oxygen from Mars air

How it works: NASA's MOXIE experiment on the Perseverance rover demonstrated a process that takes carbon dioxide from the Martian atmosphere and produces oxygen.

Why it matters: It showed that a key step toward making oxygen from local Martian resources is possible.

Engineering challenge: MOXIE was a small technology demonstration, not a full-scale system for a crewed base or a ready-made breathing supply.

🌱
FOOD PRODUCTION

Hydroponics & controlled farming

How it works: Plants grow with nutrient-rich water rather than soil. LEDs, sensors, airflow, temperature, and humidity controls create a managed growing environment.

Why it matters: Fresh crops can add variety to stored food and support research into closed-loop habitats.

Engineering challenge: Farms consume energy, water, nutrients, space, and crew time. They cannot instantly feed an entire crew.

🛡️
HABITAT PROTECTION

Regolith shielding

How it works: Robots or construction systems could place layers of lunar or Martian soil over or around a habitat to add mass between the crew and some radiation sources.

Why it matters: Local soil may reduce the need to transport all shielding material from Earth.

Engineering challenge: Shielding design must consider radiation type, thickness, habitat structure, dust, excavation, and construction safety.

⚡
POWER GENERATION

Solar arrays & energy storage

How it works: Solar cells convert sunlight into electricity. Batteries store energy for darkness, peaks in demand, or temporary loss of sunlight.

Why it matters: Power runs life support, heaters, communications, computers, and greenhouses.

Engineering challenge: Lunar nights, shadows, dust, temperature, and battery mass affect reliability. A real outpost needs carefully sized backups.

☢️
STEADY POWER

Surface fission power

How it works: A compact fission system uses controlled nuclear reactions to produce heat, which is converted into electricity.

Why it matters: It could provide steady power independent of sunlight and help support long-duration operations.

Engineering challenge: Reactor safety, heat rejection, shielding, launch constraints, maintenance, and system reliability must all be addressed.

🧑‍🚀
CREW & HABITAT

Environmental control & life support

How it works: Integrated systems manage cabin pressure, oxygen, carbon dioxide removal, humidity, temperature, water, and waste.

Why it matters: A habitat must continuously maintain conditions that humans can safely live in.

Engineering challenge: Components need monitoring, spare parts, fault detection, and redundant paths because a single failure can affect several systems.

Science note: These are real technologies, experiments, and engineering approaches at different maturity levels. A technology demonstration does not mean a complete operational lunar or Martian settlement system already exists.

MISSION OPERATIONS • WHO DOES WHAT?

How the Mission Outpost is controlled.

A real outpost would use a combination of automatic systems, onboard computers, astronauts and mission controllers on Earth. No single person operates every machine manually.

📡

1. Sensors collect data

Sensors monitor cabin pressure, oxygen, carbon dioxide, temperature, water levels, power and equipment condition.

💻

2. Computers check systems

Onboard computers compare sensor readings with safe operating limits, display warnings and run routine automatic controls.

🧑‍🚀

3. Crew and controllers decide

Astronauts handle local tasks and urgent procedures. Mission controllers on Earth support planning, troubleshooting and coordination when communication is available.

⚙️

4. Equipment responds

Fans, pumps, valves, heaters, power units and communication equipment carry out commands. Sensors then check whether the response worked.

Important: Automatic controls can handle routine tasks, but astronauts and trained mission teams supervise the outpost and respond to problems. The controls shown in this website are an educational simulation, not real telemetry or flight-control commands.

ORBITBASE NEXUS • DEEP-SPACE MISSION DOSSIER


Beyond the Blue — Earth to Moon mission


Mission concept: Beyond the Blue follows a learning-mission from the living blue world of Earth to the airless, cratered Moon. It introduces the real challenges of leaving Earth's protective environment, navigating cislunar space, entering lunar orbit and preparing for surface exploration.


DESTINATION
Earth orbit → lunar orbit → MoonAVERAGE DISTANCE
384,400 km (varies during orbit)RADIO LIGHT-TIME
About 1.28 seconds one way


🌍 Departure world — Earth


Earth is the crew’s life-support reference: its atmosphere supplies breathable air, its oceans store vast amounts of liquid water, and its global magnetic field plus thick atmosphere help shield the surface from some space radiation. A spacecraft leaving Earth must carry or carefully manage essentials that our planet normally provides naturally.


  • Atmosphere: mostly nitrogen, with about 21% oxygen at sea level.
  • Water: oceans cover roughly 71% of the surface; spacecraft must recycle and conserve water.
  • Gravity: 1 g at the surface; crews experience microgravity while orbiting Earth.
  • Protection: the atmosphere and magnetic field reduce exposure to many energetic particles.


🌕 Destination world — the Moon


The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. It has almost no atmosphere, no global protective magnetic field like Earth's, and a surface shaped by ancient impacts. Its lower gravity changes how people and equipment move, while long daylight and darkness periods make energy storage and thermal control important.


  • Gravity: about one-sixth of Earth's surface gravity.
  • Surface: rocky regolith, impact craters, mountains and permanently shadowed polar regions.
  • Temperature: exposed areas experience extreme heating and cooling; habitats need insulation and thermal control.
  • Resources: water ice is present in some permanently shadowed polar regions and is a focus of exploration.
  • Communications: radio signals take roughly 1.28 seconds to travel one way at the average Earth–Moon distance.


🚀 Mission sequence


  1. Earth departure: launch and orbital manoeuvres place the spacecraft on a planned translunar trajectory.
  2. Cislunar cruise: navigation, guidance, power, thermal control and communication systems are monitored during the journey.
  3. Lunar arrival: a carefully timed manoeuvre can place the spacecraft into lunar orbit; the crew checks navigation and landing conditions.
  4. Descent preparation: landing systems, terrain information, communications and crew procedures are checked before surface operations.
  5. Surface exploration: crews and robotic systems study geology, test equipment and investigate how future habitats could operate.


🛰️ Systems that keep the mission working


Power, oxygen, water recycling, temperature control, radiation protection, navigation and communication are linked. A power shortage can affect heaters and life support; a communication interruption can delay support from Earth. The simulation turns these connections into decisions learners can explore.


This is an educational scenario, not a real-time mission tracker or a claim that a specific crewed flight is underway. Distances and travel stages are representative; actual trajectories and durations depend on mission design.
